extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Catholic theology; clergy
extracted.subtask_description: An excerpted doctrinal/theological treatment of grace, natural vs. supernatural goods, and related heresies (Pelagianism, Baianism, Jansenism), setting out theses, dogmatic statements, definitions, and theological proofs. Intended as an instructional/expository chapter about orthodoxy on grace and salutary acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis II: Fallen man ... is able to perform some naturally good works without the aid of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis II: Fallen man, whether pagan or sinner, is able to perform some naturally good works without the aid of grace. (Technically qualified as propositio certa.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof and explanatory guidance: Scripture and the Fathers admit naturally good but unmeritorious works (opera steriliter bona); examples include salutary social acts (saluting, obeying parents, succoring the needy). The Church condemned propositions asserting the contrary (e.g., Baius/Jansenius propositions). Distinctions must be drawn between supernatural meritorious acts and naturally good acts; Augustine's rhetoric can be misunderstood if one fails to distinguish metaphorical uses. The argument appeals to physical and moral capacity distinctions (Palmieri): man is physically able to perform many natural goods though not all, and historical examples of pagans showing upright lives support the possibility. Rejection of the contrary avoids heretical consequences (e.g., requiring sinners to prepare for justification by sin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of salutary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Salutary acts (actus salutares) are those directed to the attainment of sanctifying grace and the supernatural end of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subdivision and guidance: (1) acts that prepare for justification (actus simpliciter salutares), and (2) acts which, following justification, gain merits for Heaven (actus meritorii). Because of their supernatural purpose, these acts are opposed to acts that are good only in a natural way; Fathers used various phrases (agere ad salutem, agere ad iustificationem) to denote these. Distinguish salutary (supernatural) acts from naturally good but unmeritorious acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article 2: The necessity of actual grace for all salutary acts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is taught that actual (supernatural) grace is necessary for all salutary acts (those directed toward justification and sanctifying grace).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and implications: Because salutary acts aim at the supernatural end, they require supernatural aid. This doctrine is set against Pelagianism and similar errors which deny the necessity of grace. The text discusses historical condemnations of opposing propositions and distinguishes salutary acts from natural goods that do not require supernatural merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis III: Not all actions performed in the state of mortal sin are necessarily sinful because of lack of grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Thesis III (de fide): Not all actions performed by man in the state of mortal sin are sinful on account of his not being in the state of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof and guidance: The Council of Trent anathematized the view that all pre-justification works are sins. Scriptural exhortations to sinners to repent, give alms, pray, etc., imply such acts can be salutary; patristic testimony (Origen, Augustine, Prosper) supports that some acts by sinners can be good. The thesis is defended against Jansenist/Baian extremes (which claimed universal sinfulness of sinners' acts) by showing misinterpretations of patristic texts and by logical consequences (God would not command sinners to commit new sins).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pelagianism: denial of original sin and grace (heresy criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pelagianism is characterized by denial of original sin and of the necessity of grace; it holds the human will can, by natural powers, keep all God's commandments and attain holiness without divine aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: The Church condemned Pelagianism severely; Pelagianism may concede external examples/revelation but denies supernatural assistance as a necessary gift. The text uses Pelagianism as the classical counterexample to the doctrine that salutary acts require grace and summarizes why the Church rejected Pelagian claims (e.g., grace is more than mere example; justification requires the ministration of the Holy Spirit).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of fallen nature's moral power (necessity of grace for sustaining full observance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although man can perform some naturally good acts without grace, theologians hold that man cannot observe the natural law in its entirety for any considerable length of time without the aid of grace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and evidence: Arguments include concupiscence and human frailty (shortness of life, limitations of intellect), Scripture (St. Paul describing the law in his members), and conciliar teaching (Council of Trent warns the justified must fear falling without grace). The claim is formulated also in terms of temptation: man cannot overcome all grievous temptations against the moral law without divine assistance; two formulations are offered (indefinite and more specific), and objections (Ripalda, Molina) are discussed and answered by appeal to Scripture and experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between natural and supernatural love (amor Dei naturalis vs. supernatural charity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial distinction is drawn between natural love of God (amor Dei naturalis) and supernatural charity; likewise between imperfect and perfect charity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Supernatural charity (caritas) in its perfect form necessarily presupposes supernatural aid and cannot be achieved without grace. Natural affective love may be possible without grace; effective natural love (amor effectivus) that entails full observance would not. Theologians disagree on whether fallen man can elicit perfect natural charity; positions of Scotus (affirmative) and Suarez/Bellarmine (negative) are noted. Patristic citations and conciliar condemnations distinguish which senses of 'love' are meant in authoritative texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of universal necessity of prevenient or meritorious grace (critique of Vasquez/Ripalda)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories asserting that every morally good act requires a special supernatural cogitatio congrua or that Providence invariably precedes all natural good works with entitatively supernatural grace are rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: Criticisms include (1) assuming morally indifferent acts of the concrete will (which most theologians deny), (2) counterfeiting the notion of Christian grace by turning ordinary good impulses into Christ-merit-dependent grace, and (3) denying room for natural morality between morally bad acts and supernatural meritorious acts. Ripalda's stronger universality-of-grace thesis is also addressed and found wanting because it implies denial of purely natural good acts and risks allowing justification without theological faith. The text surveys theologians who accept or reject these refinements and explains why most theologians do not accept Vasquez/Ripalda.
